papers.abstract: Learning latent dynamics is fundamental to building action-conditioned world models for planning. Among existing families, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) offer a natural framework by modeling transitions directly in latent space rather than at the pixel level. However, two issues remain in JEPA-based world models: (i) physical grounding lacks explicit aggregation of temporal context and (ii) action planning always overly relies on generic sampling distributions. To this end, we propose $\mathcal{G}$-JEPA, which incorporates temporal context into physical grounding for latent world models and couples the learned models with prior-guided action planning. Specifically, during learning, we incorporate a shared causal temporal module that aggregates temporal context within observation and prediction sequences under physical state supervision, grounding both in task-relevant physical states. When planning, we further introduce action inference through stepwise conditioning of a generative action distribution on the current and goal latent representations together with their evolving discrepancy, yielding anchored proposals that guide model-based online refinement. Together, physical state supervision guides temporal representation learning, while the action prior guides search through the learned world model. Experiments demonstrate improved planning performance on manipulation tasks, including tasks with increasing temporal separation between initial and goal observations. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/myl11045/G-JEPA.
authors: Yilei Man, Yang Chen, Jingcai Guo
bullets: Addresses missing temporal context in JEPA-based physical grounding and the reliance on generic action sampling.
Uses a shared causal temporal module to aggregate observation and prediction histories under physical-state supervision.
Infers actions by conditioning a generative action distribution on current and goal latents plus their evolving discrepancy.
Combines temporally grounded representations with prior-guided online model-based refinement.
Reports improved manipulation-task planning, including tasks with larger temporal gaps between initial and goal observations.

papers.abstract: Tracking large human-motion datasets has become the dominant route to general, expressive humanoid whole-body control, but scaling across many motions is expensive. Current pipelines use model-free reinforcement learning, either merging per-motion specialists through lossy distillation, or brute-forcing a single policy with cluster-scale compute. SuperMimic amortizes learning across all motions with one differentiable world model of their shared dynamics, fit from logged transitions of a standard rigid-body simulator. The world model and the tracking policy train together in one loop, and backpropagation-through-time over short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. Fast imagined rollouts and analytic gradients make policy learning efficient. In 3 hours on a single GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs. It reduces GPU-hours by more than $1000\times$ and fails on only 25 of 129,514 benchmark motions, versus 179 failures for the baseline. After 9.8 hours on two GPUs, SuperMimic achieves zero failures. From 1 to 264 hours of motion, the world model's prediction error stays stable, and GPU-hours to a target return grow slowly. Our policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions. SuperMimic removes compute as the bottleneck to scaling humanoid whole-body control, making it practical to measure motion-tracking scaling laws.
authors: Qiayuan Liao, Yiyang Shao, Junfeng Long, Kevin Zakka, Roberto Horowitz, Pieter Abbeel, Koushil Sreenath

papers.selection_reason: Uses a differentiable world model to amortize learning across many motions, significantly reducing compute requirements for humanoid whole-body control.
papers.title: SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model
papers.tldr: SuperMimic efficiently scales humanoid whole-body motion tracking by jointly training a policy with one differentiable world model, achieving strong simulation results and physical transfer with far less compute.

papers.abstract: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.
authors: Peisong Wen, Qianqian Xu, Minye Lei, Siran Dai, Yang Liu, Qingming Huang
bullets: Addresses redundant object-structure recovery, missing temporal correspondence, and displacement-insensitive pointwise losses in dense JEPA interfaces.
Decomposes representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks, then freezes this pretrained interface for downstream use.
Introduces a Transition Memory Predictor with slot-specific and shared cross-slot dynamics, retrieving transitions through corresponding-slot statistics.
Uses Unbalanced Optimal Transport to supervise mask prediction and compare predicted and goal masks based on spatial progress.
Features transfer across seven visual-understanding benchmarks and improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar and four robotic-arm tasks on REALM-JEPA.

papers.abstract: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.
authors: Zhiyuan Liu, Sicheng Liu, Haiyu Wu
bullets: Addresses multimodal futures, where one observation can lead to several valid continuations.

papers.abstract: Action-free videos are an appealing substitute for costly teleoperated data. Latent action models (LAMs) turn videos into a supervision signal by inferring abstract actions between frames. Existing LAMs observe a single camera view, which resolves 6D robot actions only ambiguously missing out-of-plane movements and potential occlusions. We propose a LAM that ingests synchronized multi-camera views using cross-attention to resolve depth and occlusions before compressing them into latent actions. The latent actions are fed into a policy in which a latent expert and an action expert are coupled by sequential flow matching around a frozen VLM backbone. We further evaluate in strict cross-embodiment settings where task-specific demonstrations come from other embodiments. We show that dual-view LAM pretraining improves the decodability of ground-truth 6D actions by 17% compared to single-view, while scaling single-view data by two orders of magnitude is not sufficient to fully recover out-of-plane motions. The downstream policy improves success rate by +13.5% compared to +6.2% for single-view LAM. A single cross-embodiment is sufficient for skill transfer, and adding a second viewpoint outperforms adding up to four further embodiments. The results transfer to hardware where demonstrations come from a human hand improving success rate by +20% over action-only policies in 850 rollouts. We show that video and robot data are complementary, and that benefits of learning from video are task-dependent. Website: https://learnsyslab.github.io/multiview_latent_action_pretraining/
authors: Oliver Hausd\"orfer, Felix Minzenmay, Mani Majd, Maximilian P. Christof, Shiyuan Zhang, Angela P. Schoellig
bullets: Single-view latent action models ambiguously infer 6D movements, especially out-of-plane actions and occluded interactions.
The proposed model combines cross-attention over multiple views with sequential flow matching between latent and action experts around a frozen VLM.
Dual-view pretraining improves 6D-action decodability by 17% over single-view and yields a +13.5% downstream success-rate gain versus +6.2% for single-view.
One cross-embodiment source is sufficient for skill transfer; adding a second viewpoint is more beneficial than adding up to four additional embodiments.
Hardware experiments using human-hand demonstrations improve success by 20% over action-only policies across 850 rollouts, with benefits varying by task.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Method: We combine latent action pretraining from in-domain cross-embodiment videos with a downstream flow-matching policy. First, latent actions are inferred from a large cross-embodiment video dataset. Second, a sequential policy is learned on the latent actions and a small set of demonstrations on the target embodiment. The LAM uses a spatio-temporal transformer to merge multiple viewpoints before computing the latents. The spatial block attends to patches of other viewpoints, yielding latent actions grounded in 3D space. Latent action labels and real robot actions are jointly used to train a hierarchical downstream policy. The policy uses sequential flow matching experts and outputs actions applied to the robot.
Fig. 8. Failure modes. Models struggle with object grasping (44% of failure cases). The push task requires precision to align the gripper with the milk.

Fig. 4. Real World Tasks: We evaluate the policies and skill-transfer on six tasks consisting of novel movements, novel background, novel objects, and novel placements. For each eval task, we collect 50 human demonstrations and evaluate under settings with 0–50 robot demonstrations per task. papers.abstract: Latent world models let an agent plan in latent space. The planner searches for an action sequence that minimizes a cost, and that cost is often the $\ell_2$ distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent. The latent, however, is partly noise: the regularizer that prevents collapse during world model training promotes variance in the directions carrying no signal. We show that the same regularizer also supplies the structure to prune that noise in the latent. SIGReg drives the latent marginal to a standard Gaussian at every step, and assuming further that the latent sequence is a Gauss-Markov process, the transition is linear with its covariance pinned by the map itself, $z' \mid z \sim \mathcal{N}(Az,\, I - AA^\top)$. Fitting the state dynamics $A$ therefore yields the covariance at no additional cost, and in its eigenbasis each latent direction carries its own uncertainty. Furthermore, constraining $A$ to be a normal matrix fixes that basis across timesteps, so one eigenbasis measures the uncertainty over an arbitrary number of steps and serves as a stable basis to compute the planning cost on. We then restrict the $\ell_2$ cost to the $k$-dimensional subspace the state dynamics carry forward with the least uncertainty. The correction is post hoc: the encoder, the predictor, the rollout, and the planner are all left untouched, and only a single constrained matrix, $A$, is fit. We evaluate across six environments and show large gains on the 2D navigation tasks, TwoRoom and PointMaze, raising success rate over the plain $\ell_2$ cost by up to $+54.7$ points under a harder planning setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yjang43/lp2.
bullets: Latent world-model planning often uses terminal ℓ2 distance, but learned latents contain noise in directions unrelated to task signal.
The method fits a constrained normal transition matrix under a Gauss-Markov assumption to derive a stable uncertainty basis across timesteps.
Planning cost is restricted to the k-dimensional subspace propagated with the least uncertainty; the encoder, predictor, rollout, and planner remain unchanged.
Across six environments, the approach shows its largest gains on TwoRoom and PointMaze, improving success by up to 54.7 percentage points in a harder setting.
Scope: effectiveness is especially demonstrated on 2D navigation tasks and depends on the stated Gaussian and Gauss-Markov assumptions.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation is not merely observation-to-action generation, but the realization of task-specified state changes in the physical world. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) methods directly learn observation-to-action mappings, imposing a substantial learning burden due to the gap between semantic understanding and action execution. Although world-action models (WAMs) improve control through future prediction, modeling complete future states wastes capacity on static appearance and action-irrelevant changes. We propose Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA), a paradigm that reformulates full future prediction as compact actionable transition modeling. Its core is a compact Delta variable that captures latent world-state changes, serving as an interface between vision-language understanding and action generation. VLDA learns Delta through a unified objective composed of the Local Transition Filter (LT-Filter) and Global Transition Anchor (GT-Anchor). LT-Filter captures task-relevant manipulation-centric changes while suppressing static reconstruction biases. GT-Anchor provides coarse future-level regularization to preserve the overall direction of state changes. Delta-Driven Action Refinement (DDAR) further grounds Delta in the action manifold and injects it as a structured seed to guide action denoising. We implement VLDA within LoongForge, an open-source training framework for large-scale foundation and embodied models, using its modular and distributed infrastructure for unified two-stage optimization. Experiments show that VLDA improves long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization, validating actionable Delta as an alternative to direct action prediction and full future-state modeling.
authors: Lingsen Zhang, Wei Li, Jie He, Henghua Zhang, Kai Mo, Shiyong Li, Yanpeng Wang, Rui Shao
bullets: Targets the learning burden and semantic-to-action gap in direct vision-language-action policies.
Models actionable state changes instead of reconstructing complete future states, reducing focus on static or irrelevant details.
Combines LT-Filter for local manipulation changes with GT-Anchor for coarse future-direction regularization.
Uses DDAR to inject the learned Delta into action denoising as a structured action-space seed.
Experiments report improved long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization.],

papers.abstract: Latent world models such as LeWM plan by searching for an action sequence whose predicted terminal latent is closest to the goal latent under an ambient norm, such as the Euclidean distance. Planning with such a cost assumes that proximity in the ambient latent space reflects proximity to the goal in the environment. Studying LeWM, we find that this assumption holds only in a small neighborhood around the goal, whereas farther away the L2 cost forms spurious low-cost basins that trap the planner. Yet neighborhood-based embeddings show that the latents retain the underlying physical state. We therefore hypothesize that the latents lie near a curved, low-dimensional manifold, and that the terminal cost should measure the distance along this latent manifold rather than through the ambient space. To estimate this manifold distance, we propose the Neighborhood Graph Cost (NGC), which computes shortest-path distances on a mutual nearest-neighbor graph constructed over training latents. NGC changes only the terminal cost and requires no retraining. This single change improves the planning success rate of LeWM across all four benchmark tasks and nearly solves TwoRoom and Reacher: even at the farthest goal offsets tested, NGC reaches 95% and 100% success, whereas the L2 cost falls to 27% and 81%. These results support the manifold hypothesis and our argument that latent world models should plan with distances along the latent manifold.
authors: Zunzhi You, Linwei Tao, Siyu Xu, Yunke Wang, Chang Xu
bullets: Ambient L2 terminal costs work near the goal but create misleading low-cost basins farther away.
Latent representations retain physical state while apparently lying near a curved, low-dimensional manifold.

Scope: evidence is reported for LeWM and four benchmark tasks; NGC relies on the training-latent neighborhood graph.

papers.abstract: Learning a single perceptive policy for diverse humanoid loco-manipulation requires unifying high-level task decisions without losing the state-dependent physical responses that make each interaction succeed. This makes the representation between high-level planning and whole-body control critical: kinematic or contact targets provide compact abstractions but do not directly encode interaction-specific control responses, while directly predicting low-level actions requires the planner to model high-frequency closed-loop feedback. We propose FIBER, a framework that uses the executable latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM) as a shared planning representation for heterogeneous interaction skills. Our latent policy projection (LPP) maps independently acquired task-specific policies into this representation by identifying latent commands whose induced actions match their local control responses, enabling lower-rate planning while retaining the BFM's high-frequency state feedback. After projection, we aggregate closed-loop latent rollouts from all skills and train a single perceptive flow planner entirely offline. We further introduce AH-BFM, an adaptive-horizon BFM trained with multi-gamma forward-backward (FB) learning to support both precise control and temporally extended whole-body behavior. We evaluate FIBER on box pickup, door opening, and object grasping in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Across 128 diverse variations per task in simulation, FIBER achieves 42.0% mean success, more than tripling projected latent replay (11.6%) and substantially outperforming kinematic planning (3.5%). Real-world experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering through the same unified planner.
authors: Yutang Lin, Guanya Shi, C. Karen Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of unifying task-level planning with interaction-specific, state-dependent whole-body control.
Projects independently learned skill policies into the latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM).
Trains a single offline perceptive flow planner on aggregated closed-loop latent rollouts from multiple skills.
Introduces AH-BFM with adaptive horizons for both precise control and extended whole-body behavior.
Across three simulated tasks, achieves 42.0% mean success versus 11.6% for latent replay and 3.5% for kinematic planning; real-robot tests show transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of FIBER. (a) Heterogeneous interaction experts are acquired through motion imitation, reward shaping, or successorfeature-guided behavior reuse. (b) Action-aligned latent policy projection maps their short-horizon control responses into a frozen adaptivehorizon BFM; closed-loop rollouts produce executable latent trajectories. (c) These trajectories train a unified perceptive planner entirely offline. Language commands or waypoint conditions are encoded as steering tokens, and a DiT planner predicts future latent trajectories. During deployment, the planner replans from onboard observations while the frozen BFM provides high-frequency feedback.

Fig. 4: Qualitative real-world behaviors of FIBER. (a) During box carrying, the robot reacts to an unstable grasp by briefly lifting the box and repositioning its hands underneath for more secure support, illustrating high-frequency closed-loop adjustment. (b) After picking up the box, the same policy follows waypoint commands while carrying it; after stumbling, the robot stabilizes on its knees and recovers before continuing, demonstrating interaction-preserving skill chaining, steering, and recovery. (c) For a heavy door, the robot leans its whole body into the interaction to generate sufficient pushing force, showing adaptive whole-body realization of contact-rich tasks.

Fig. 3: Skill chaining with FIBER. In a single rollout, the policy sequentially opens the door in (i), picks up the box in (ii), and carries it back through the doorway in (iii), demonstrating closed-loop chaining of multiple interaction skills under changing high-level commands.

papers.abstract: Reliable long-horizon prediction remains a central challenge for embodied world models. Although recent generative models can synthesize visually plausible action-conditioned futures, their latent dynamics are typically learned through unconstrained transition modules, which may gradually deviate from coherent physical evolution as predictions are recursively rolled forward. We investigate whether explicitly structuring latent state evolution can improve the stability and utility of such imagined trajectories. To this end, we introduce HWM, a structured dynamics framework that represents backbone latents in a learned phase space consisting of generalized coordinates and momenta. Future states are propagated through dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics and mapped back to the original latent representation through a learnable inverse interface. The resulting formulation can be integrated into existing world-model architectures without redesigning their perception or decoding components, while multi-step transition supervision encourages the structured rollout to remain aligned with the latent trajectories induced by real observations. Controlled simulation experiments show that HWM produces more accurate estimates of velocity, acceleration, and jerk and substantially reduces long-horizon energy drift relative to unstructured latent dynamics. We further evaluate the approach across three distinct embodied world-model settings, covering single-arm multi-view prediction with Ctrl-World, dual-arm single-view prediction with EVAC, and task-oriented single-arm prediction with Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B. On RoboCasa, incorporating HWM into Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B yields a 2.7% relative improvement in task success. On real-world AgiBot World trajectories, it improves nDTW by 9.7% with Ctrl-World and Logic by 8.4% with EVAC.
authors: Kevin Chen, Yu-Wei Zhan, Haoran Liang, Sen Cui, Changshui Zhang
bullets: Problem: Unconstrained latent transitions can drift from coherent physical evolution during recursive long-horizon prediction.
Method: Represent latent states with generalized coordinates and momenta, propagate them using dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics, and map them back through a learnable inverse interface.
Training integration: HWM can augment existing world models without changing their perception or decoding components, while multi-step supervision aligns imagined and observed latent trajectories.
Results: HWM improves velocity, acceleration, and jerk estimates and reduces long-horizon energy drift in controlled simulations.
Embodied evaluations show gains across three settings, including 2.7% higher task success on RoboCasa, 9.7% higher nDTW with Ctrl-World, and 8.4% higher Logic with EVAC.

papers.abstract: A key design choice in visual world models is what information the latent state is encouraged to preserve. Models that learn a latent space with only a latent-prediction objective adapt to environment dynamics, but the predictive objective alone admits collapsed solutions and provides no explicit constraint on the visual information retained by the latent. Models built directly on pretrained visual features inherit a strong visual prior, but tie prediction and planning to a frozen state space. We propose Anchor-WM, which instead uses pretrained visual features as a teacher for learning a compact latent state rather than as the world-model state itself. Anchor-WM learns this compact latent with action-conditioned dynamics, while distilling the dense DINO representations through a training-only distillation head. This encourages the compact latent to retain visual information captured by the pretrained representation while discouraging representational collapse. At inference, the DINO encoder and distillation head are discarded, allowing prediction and planning to operate entirely in the learned latent space. Anchor-WM achieves the best average success rate across the four evaluated environments while enabling substantially faster planning than world models operating directly on DINO patch features. These results show that pretrained visual features can effectively guide world-model learning without defining the state space used for prediction and planning.
authors: Yanbo Wang, Nan Lin, Wendelin B\"ohmer, Javier Alonso-Mora
bullets: Addresses latent-state collapse and the loss of visual information in prediction-only world models.
Learns an action-conditioned compact latent while distilling dense DINO representations through a temporary training head.
Discards the DINO encoder and distillation head at inference, enabling planning entirely in the learned latent space.
Achieves the best average success rate across four evaluated environments and substantially faster planning than models using DINO patch features.
Shows that pretrained visual features can guide, rather than define, the state space for visual world models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Training and inference of Anchor-WM. During training, the observation encoder Eθ, transition model Tϕ, and distillation head Hψ are optimized jointly, while the pretrained DINO encoder remains frozen. The compact latent is trained with both a dynamics prediction objective and a distillation objective that reconstructs DINO features. At inference, the DINO encoder and distillation head are discarded, and planning is performed entirely in the learned latent space by optimizing an action sequence whose predicted terminal latent approaches the encoded goal latent.

Figure 4: Open-Loop Rollouts on PushT and Cube. DINO-WM produces visually sharper reconstructions, whereas Anchor-WM discards some fine-grained appearance information. Nevertheless, Anchor-WM preserves the task-relevant evolution of object configurations and interactions. papers.abstract: We present RhinoNet, a simplicial complex-based point cloud neural network, that creates a geometry-preserving embedding of high-dimensional point clouds. RhinoNet takes collections of datasets, also called {\em data cohorts}, and processes each dataset (point cloud) within the cohort as a simplicial complex. These simplicial complexes have datapoints as vertices and edges learned by Vietoris-Rips filtration. Using simplicial wavelets and MLP layers, RhinoNet computes a vector representation of each dataset in a latent space produced by an autoencoder. The latent space is optimized such that an optimal transport distance between pairs of point clouds is preserved between the latent representations. We apply RhinoNet to single-cell datasets collected on patients---a common source of such high-dimensional data. RhinoNet creates a patient level representation, known in biological contexts as a phenoscape. We establish that RhinoNet generates organized phenoscapes, whereas other methods such as static maps do not. Next we show that we can generate entire point clouds by sampling and decoding this phenoscape. We show two modes of generation via 1) latent flow matching and 2) geodesic interpolation in latent space, followed by a decoding back into the point cloud space. RhinoNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on single-cell and spatial data cohorts relative to tested baselines. Overall, RhinoNet lifts the concepts of representation learning and generative modeling to the point cloud or population level and defines a neural model for phenoscaping.
authors: Siddharth Viswanath, Hiren Madhu, Eddie Cavallin, Benjamin Jones, Alistair Wilkinson, Christopher Tape, Michael Perlmutter, Rex Ying, Ian Adelstein, Smita Krishnaswamy
bullets: Processes each dataset as a Vietoris–Rips simplicial complex with datapoints as vertices and learned edges.
Uses simplicial wavelets, MLP layers, and an autoencoder to encode datasets into a latent phenoscape.
Optimizes latent representations to preserve optimal-transport distances between point clouds.
Generates point clouds through latent flow matching or geodesic interpolation followed by decoding.
Applied to single-cell and spatial data cohorts, achieving state-of-the-art performance against tested baselines and producing organized phenoscap es.

papers.abstract: Visual navigation requires goal directed planning informed by predictions of environment dynamics. Representative navigation world model methods propose complete action candidates before predicting consequences for selection or search updates. For each candidate, predictions primarily evaluate proposed actions rather than guide its stepwise construction. To this end, we propose InJepa, an intention first planning paradigm centered on latent states. A goal conditioned JEPA proposes latent intentions, and an action conditioned JEPA continually predicts future latent states. Both operate in a shared latent space to align their predictive representations. Within each candidate, predicted consequences feed into the next intention proposal and action inference, forming a closed loop of intention, action, and consequence. This extends the world model's role beyond evaluation to leading candidate construction through latent intentions. We evaluate InJepa through closed loop image goal navigation in Habitat MP3D. The results show effective multistep navigation through intention guided action generation and consequence feedback. Experiments across encoders further support applicability across visual representations. These findings support latent intentions as the central planning object and show that world models can directly guide plan construction through coordinated reasoning about intentions and consequences. Code is available at https://github.com/zhuxun132/InJepa.
authors: Siming Zhou, Bowen Ma, Ruiran Du, Pengcheng Zheng, Sheng Zheng, Dongshen Han, Zhijie Li, Wei Dong, Fan Mo, Chaoning Zhang

Feeds predicted consequences back into subsequent intention proposals and action inference in a closed loop.
Evaluated on closed-loop image-goal navigation in Habitat MP3D, demonstrating effective multistep navigation.
Results across encoders support applicability across different visual representations.

papers.abstract: Latent world models learn action-conditioned state transitions in a compact representation space, providing a predictive model for visual planning and control. However, planning with these models typically requires costly test-time optimization over action sequences. We propose to replace this online search with a goal-conditioned inverse model that directly predicts actions from current and goal observations. A key challenge is that action prediction alone neither ensures that goal representations encode action-relevant information nor that predicted actions are consistent with the learned latent prediction model. We introduce Hindsight Inverse JEPA Planning (HIJP), a search-free framework that addresses both aspects during training. HIJP relabels future observations along offline trajectories as goals, providing action supervision across multiple temporal horizons. By retaining gradients through the goal representations, this supervision directly shapes the visual representation. HIJP further feeds predicted actions into the latent predictor model and aligns the resulting next-state representations with encoded successor observations, enforcing action-transition consistency. At inference time, the inverse dynamics model and latent predictor models are applied alternately to generate multi-step action sequences without online search. Across four visual control tasks, HIJP achieves 86.8% overall success and a 1.9-16.5x planning speedup over search-based planning.
authors: Guanchen Du, Jinhao Du, Yanpeng Sun, Shan Zhang, Na Zhao, Zechao Li
bullets: Latent world-model planning usually requires costly test-time optimization over action sequences.
HIJP uses future observations as hindsight goals to train an inverse model across multiple planning horizons.
Gradients through goal representations make visual features more action-relevant.

Across four visual control tasks, HIJP reaches 86.8% overall success and provides a 1.9–16.5× planning speedup over search-based methods.

papers.abstract: Many vision-language-action policies rely on action-labeled robot demonstrations and lack an explicit mechanism for predicting future visual states. These limitations hinder learning from action-free videos and can encourage overfitting to demonstration conditions, weakening generalization and robustness. We present TS-WAM, a lightweight Teacher-Student World-Action Model that addresses these challenges through self-supervised temporal learning and explicit future prediction. Its vlm-jepa framework learns from heterogeneous data, including robot demonstrations and action-free human videos, using an EMA target branch without requiring a separately trained external teacher. By coupling vlm-jepa with delta-lwm, TS-WAM learns to predict latent actions from the current observation and instruction and uses them to predict future visual features that guide action generation at inference. A unified end-to-end training architecture jointly optimizes temporal representation learning, visual dynamics, and robot control without a separate latent-action or world-model pretraining stage. The EMA target branch is removed at inference, keeping the deployed policy lightweight. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with real-world manipulation experiments on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate that TS-WAM achieves strong manipulation performance, generalization, and robustness.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are typically trained with action prediction as the primary supervision signal, since robots ultimately execute actions. Auxiliary objectives such as latent-action (LA) and future-vision (FV) prediction are often added to improve policy learning, yet they compete with action prediction for the same training budget. We ask whether, under a fixed budget, allocating a substantial share of training samples to such objectives, rather than to further action prediction, can improve policy learning. We build a unified VLA framework that couples a two-stream multimodal diffusion transformer (MMDiT) with a sample-level router, which assigns each training sample to either action prediction or an auxiliary objective and thus makes supervision allocation explicit. Within this framework, we instantiate three LA targets based on LAPA and its DINO-feature variants, and three FV targets based on DINOv3, V-JEPA 2, and Wan2.2 representations. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, and four real-robot tasks, suitable LA and FV supervision outperforms action-only training under the same budget, even when action prediction receives no more than half of the training samples. FV generally outperforms LA, although the strongest LA target remains competitive on CALVIN. Diagnostic analyses suggest that DINO-based LA targets emphasize relative motion, whereas FV targets emphasize absolute position and task identity. We therefore argue that what robot policies learn to predict, and how training is allocated among these targets, should be treated as explicit design choices rather than defaulting to action-dominant training.
authors: Haitao Shen, Hanyu Liu, Yihan Lin, Huiping Liu, Junbo Cui, Daoheng Li, Yang Li, Jing Zhang, Wenxin Li, Yuan Yao

Suitable auxiliary supervision outperforms action-only training, even when action prediction receives at most half the samples; future-vision generally performs best.
DINO-based latent-action targets emphasize relative motion, while future-vision targets emphasize absolute position and task identity.

papers.abstract: Understanding the objectives that drive agents' behavior is crucial in strategic environments, where multiple agents interact and adapt to one another. This challenge arises in domains such as cybersecurity, autonomous driving, and online markets, where agents' underlying incentives are typically unknown and must be inferred from their observed behavior. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a natural framework for this problem, but extending IRL to strategic multi-agent settings introduces a fundamental challenge: a reward that explains observed behavior does not necessarily induce optimal strategies when used for decision-making. In this work, we study this problem through the lens of \emph{strategic identifiability}, and show that learning from a fixed policy pair can be insufficient to strategically identify rewards, independent of the number of expert samples $K$. Motivated by this, we introduce an active IRL algorithm for two-player repeated Stackelberg games, in which the leader adaptively selects policies to elicit informative responses about the follower's reward. Combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, we derive finite-sample guarantees on the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, matching up to polylogarithmic factors a new minimax learning rate of $K^{-1/2}$. Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.
authors: Antoine Bergerault, Cyrille Kone, Giorgia Ramponi
bullets: Strategic multi-agent IRL is challenging because rewards that explain observed behavior may not produce optimal decisions.
The paper formalizes this issue through strategic identifiability and shows that observing a fixed policy pair may be insufficient, regardless of the number of expert samples.
It introduces an active IRL algorithm for repeated two-player Stackelberg games, combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design.
Finite-sample guarantees achieve a Stackelberg sub-optimality rate matching the minimax rate up to polylogarithmic factors.
Experiments in an anti-poaching setting show benefits from active exploration for reward recovery and strategic performance.

papers.abstract: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) addresses decision-making under uncertainty and adverse outcomes. Learning risk-sensitive policies from fixed datasets is important when additional interaction with the environment is costly. Existing work on risk-sensitive RL focuses on online settings or specific risk measures, leaving a general theoretical understanding of its offline setting underdeveloped. In this work, we investigate efficient offline risk-sensitive RL using the optimized certainty equivalent (OCE), a general class of risk measures. We consider two formulations: dynamic-OCE RL, which applies OCE recursively at each step, and static-OCE RL, which applies a single OCE to the cumulative rewards. Under the tabular setting, we develop pessimistic value-iteration algorithms for both formulations and establish tight sublinear suboptimality bounds, explicitly capturing how risk sensitivity, encoded by utility functions, affects learning difficulty. Moreover, we establish minimax suboptimality lower bounds to characterize the problem's fundamental limits. To handle large state spaces, we further develop pessimistic least-squares value-iteration algorithms that incorporate the general OCE risk criterion into linear function approximation. We establish utility-dependent sublinear guarantees with explicit dependence on the feature dimension $d$. To our knowledge, we provide the first offline algorithms along with the first upper and lower suboptimality bounds for both dynamic- and static-OCE RL.
authors: Hanzhen Wang, Boxiang Lyu, Zhongxiang Dai, Siyang Gao, Dake Zhang, Shuang Qiu
bullets: Addresses offline risk-sensitive RL, where further environment interaction is costly and existing theory is limited beyond specific risk measures.
Studies both dynamic-OCE RL, applying risk recursively, and static-OCE RL, applying one OCE to cumulative rewards.
Proposes pessimistic value-iteration algorithms for tabular problems and pessimistic least-squares value iteration for large state spaces with linear function approximation.
Provides utility-dependent sublinear upper bounds and minimax lower bounds, including explicit effects of risk sensitivity and feature dimension.
Claims the first offline algorithms and upper/lower suboptimality bounds for both dynamic- and static-OCE RL.

papers.abstract: Learning intrinsic dynamics---the relationship between actions and their consequences---is essential for world models. However, visual variations unrelated to the underlying control process can obscure this relationship in learned representations. We investigate the connection between action predictability, defined as the ability to reconstruct an action from consecutive latent states, and the preservation of intrinsic dynamics. Our central hypothesis is that encouraging action predictability discourages representations from discarding the distinctions between different actions and their consequences. We provide two complementary forms of evidence for this connection. Theoretically, we derive a positive lower bound on squared inverse prediction error when the encoder merges distinguishable outcomes of different actions from the same state and appearance, and show that forward prediction can still be exact on those transitions. Empirically, controlled appearance-diversity comparisons, supervision interventions, and latent probes support the role of action prediction in preserving control-relevant transition information. We instantiate action predictability with Concat IDM, which predicts actions from concatenated latent states and updates the shared encoder using action labels already available in offline trajectories, without changing the test-time planner. Across three independent training runs on Push-T with 24 appearances, Concat IDM increases planning success from 9.1% to 77.2%; its paired improvement is 52.9 percentage points larger than that observed with a single appearance. Together, these findings support action predictability as an inductive bias toward intrinsic dynamics and demonstrate the practical benefits of Concat IDM for latent planning under visual diversity.
authors: Jiamin Shi, Yuanhong Zhang, Zhiyang Liu, Jiawei Sun, Jingwen Fu
bullets: Visual changes unrelated to control can cause representations to discard distinctions between actions and their consequences.
The paper links reconstructing actions from consecutive latent states to preserving intrinsic dynamics, with theoretical and empirical support.
Concat IDM predicts actions from concatenated latent states and trains the shared encoder using action labels from offline trajectories.
On Push-T with 24 appearances, Concat IDM raises planning success from 9.1% to 77.2%; the reported gain is larger than with a single appearance.
Scope: evidence focuses on latent planning under visual diversity and the Push-T evaluation setting.

papers.abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) can capture manipulation priors from action-free videos, but discrete latents usually impose a granularity bottleneck, limiting their ability to represent fine-grained action. Recent continuous alternatives mitigate this, but they are typically used as proxies for world modeling and require a further planning step to produce executable actions. We thus introduce UniLAP, a unified continuous latent-action policy that models the latent space via flow matching and bypasses reliance on future frames during inference. By distilling a LAM teacher with a flow-adaptive objective, UniLAP inherits the teacher's action representation while retaining the multimodal distribution of feasible behaviors. To decouple latent representations from task-irrelevant appearance, we extract a label-free motion target to isolate relevant kinematic cues from spurious visual dynamics. With the established embodiment-agnostic latent manifold, UniLAP can be easily adapted to novel platforms. Pretrained on multi-source videos at a compact 1.1B parameter scale, UniLAP outperforms state-of-the-art latent-action and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) baselines across hand pose forecasting, single-arm and humanoid manipulation, and real-world deployment.
bullets: Addresses the granularity limits of discrete latent actions and the extra planning required by continuous world-modeling approaches.

Extracts label-free motion targets to separate task-relevant kinematics from task-irrelevant appearance.
Builds an embodiment-agnostic latent manifold that adapts to new robotic platforms.
At 1.1B parameters, outperforms latent-action and VLA baselines across pose forecasting, single-arm and humanoid manipulation, and real-world deployment.

papers.abstract: World-action models aim to turn visual anticipation into driving decisions, yet typically train action experts on trajectory representations defined independently of visual dynamics. This motivates deriving action targets directly from visual motion. We first examine a simpler setting in which trajectories are reconstructed from recorded future images. Even without the need for future prediction, reconstruction captures the dominant maneuver but leaves centimeter-scale errors. We therefore introduce VITAL (Vision-Induced Tokens for Action Learning), an action tokenizer that couples a visually derived motion scaffold with a compact residual encoding the trajectory error left by that scaffold. This representation makes visual motion the principal prediction target and gives small metric corrections a separate, normalized learning scale. Using flow matching, the action expert jointly predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command, without generating future images at inference. The same residual coordinates support bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the predicted visual scaffold fixed. With only one action denoising step, VITAL achieves 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, within 0.13 points of its ten-step score at 3.29x the end-to-end inference speed. Without retraining, it achieves 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and 38.6 on navhard. Project page: https://worldbench.github.io/vital
authors: Ao Liang, Youquan Liu, Mingxiao Li, Wei Chow, Lingdong Kong, Yue Liao, Dongyue Lu, Yu Yang, Wei Yin, Runnan Chen
bullets: Addresses trajectory errors caused by action representations that are disconnected from visual dynamics.
Uses a visually derived motion scaffold plus a compact residual encoding for centimeter-scale corrections.
A flow-matching action expert predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command.
Supports bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the visual scaffold fixed.
Reaches 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 with one denoising step, near its ten-step score at 3.29× higher end-to-end speed; also reports 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 38.6 on navhard.

papers.abstract: Learning world models across diverse domains calls for a unified control space, yet ac- tion interfaces vary across domains and action annotations are often scarce. Latent ac- tions learned directly from videos offer a promising way to establish such a space without explicit action supervision. However, learning shared latent actions across domains re- mains challenging, as variations in appearance, embodiment, and dynamics can entangle domain-specific visual cues with transferable transition structure. To this end, we intro- duce OneLA, a simple framework that learns continuous latent actions through a shared orthogonal dictionary and a common predictive objective, without task-specific designs or cross-domain alignment losses during latent action pretraining. These latent actions pro- vide a shared conditioning interface for world models, with lightweight adapters mapping native control commands into the same space. Conditioned on latent actions and the cur- rent visual state, the world model predicts context-dependent transitions for controllable rollout. OneLA improves action readout across domains and reduces action cycle-transfer rotation error by 24.8% over the strongest evaluated baseline. A joint-training comparison further shows a 20.5% improvement in Human Preference Score v3 (HPSv3) for real- scene generation. These results suggest a path toward general-purpose world models that learn from diverse videos and support flexible control through latent action space.
authors: Ziyu Zhu, Zhaoxu Sun, Fan Jiang, Chiyu Wang, Junfeng Ni, Mu Xu

Improves action readout and reduces action cycle-transfer rotation error by 24.8% over the strongest evaluated baseline.
Joint training improves HPSv3 by 20.5% for real-scene generation.

papers.abstract: Robotic ultrasound can standardize image acquisition and reduce operator workload and variability, but policy learning remains limited by the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments. While controllable world models have advanced rapidly in natural-image domains, ultrasound world modeling remains challenging because each frame captures only a cross-section of unobserved 3D anatomy, causing small probe motions to induce large appearance changes. Existing approaches rely on robot-tracked poses and latent-space prediction, but do not directly generate the observations required for interactive control. We propose SonoWorld, a causal ultrasound world model that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them to 6-DoF control using a small set of freehand clinical scans tracked with an EM sensor. SonoWorld is trained in three stages: pretraining a latent-action-conditioned video diffusion model on around 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames; grounding the learned video dynamics to metric probe poses with a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset; and applying distribution matching distillation to enable causal, long-horizon autoregressive generation with selectively caching eviction tokens at inference time. We evaluate controllability through pose-following fidelity, round-trip consistency, and axis-specific control under synthetic actions on held-out tracked scans, and further validate it with a user study. In model-based action discrimination, SonoWorld correctly ranks the target-directed probe motion over an equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials. To our knowledge, SonoWorld is the first causal, pose-controllable ultrasound world model learned primarily from freehand clinical videos, providing a data-driven interactive environment for robotic ultrasound data acquisition and policy evaluation.
authors: Zefan Yang, Zheyuan Zhang, Boris Maihe, Yikang Liu, Hang Yu, Ankush Mukherjee, Xiao Chen, Pingkun Yan, Terrence Chen, Shanhui Sun
bullets: Addresses the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments for robotic ultrasound, where small probe motions can cause large image changes.
Learns video dynamics from about 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames and grounds them to 6-DoF probe poses using a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset.
Uses staged training with latent-action-conditioned video diffusion, pose grounding, and distribution-matching distillation for causal long-horizon generation.
Evaluated pose-following, round-trip consistency, axis-specific control, and user-study performance on held-out tracked scans.
Correctly ranked target-directed motion over equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials.

papers.abstract: A robot needs a world model that predicts how its actions will change the scene and a policy that chooses those actions. Models are usually built and evaluated for only one of these roles, and every robot records its actions in its own format. We ask whether one robot world model can serve both roles across different bodies, and what makes this work. We present GreenWAM, a world foundation model for robotics, together with the recipe that produces it: (1) a shared anatomical action space that describes 20 robot families, from bimanual arms to dexterous humanoids, in common joint coordinates; (2) joint training on these families in visual, action-conditioned and world-action modes; and (3) policies that split an action expert off the generator. As a world model, GreenWAM attains top-tier trajectory, depth and 3D accuracy on WorldArena 1.0, ahead of every world-action model and video generator in our comparison. As a policy, it scores among the top entries of the RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard, reaches the highest zero-shot LIBERO-plus success among the compared methods and is competitive with dedicated vision-language-action and world-action policies on CALVIN and LIBERO. We further adapt GreenWAM to a real humanoid, where it succeeds more often than policies adapted from $\pi_{0.5}$ and from Cosmos 3 Edge, and distill it into a single-step policy for real-time control. Controlled experiments yield three findings: robot specialization improves world prediction and control together; an action expert helps when split off at the start of adaptation; and keeping world-model modes during policy adaptation preserves robustness to scene changes.
authors: Gennady Sidorov, Valerii Kornilov, Denis Grankin, Polina Fedotova, Aleksey Postnikov
bullets: Addresses the challenge of building one model for robots with different bodies and action formats.
Uses a shared anatomical action space covering 20 robot families and trains jointly in visual, action-conditioned, and world-action modes.
Separates an action expert from the generator to derive policies, including a distilled single-step policy for real-time control.
Achieves top-tier WorldArena 1.0 world-model accuracy and strong results across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-plus, CALVIN, and LIBERO.
Real-robot adaptation to a humanoid outperforms the cited adapted baselines; specialization and retaining world-model modes improve robustness.

papers.title: GreenWAM: A World Foundation Model for Robotics
papers.tldr: GreenWAM is a cross-robot world foundation model that supports both scene prediction and action selection through shared actions, joint training, and adaptable policies.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform manipulation tasks using camera images and language instructions, but object slip or visual occlusion can disrupt execution. Recovery is typically learned during policy training or delegated to a monitor that triggers a scripted repair after detecting a failure. We introduce ForkCast, a predictive recovery framework that compares counterfactual futures to determine whether and how to intervene in a frozen VLA policy. At each decision point, ForkCast evaluates three candidates: executing the policy's nominal action chunk (Commit), adjusting the camera viewpoint (Reobserve), and replanning the arm trajectory (Replan). A candidate-conditioned world model forecasts the latent outcome of each candidate at a common future horizon, and a shared task-progress head scores the predicted outcomes. By evaluating the policy's own continuation alongside the repair candidates, a single comparison based on task progress determines both whether and how to intervene, without a failure detector, an intervention threshold, or updates to the VLA backbone. On five simulated RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with injected occlusion and object slip, ForkCast increases pooled success from 13.3% for the frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ policy to 30.0% and transfers to two additional VLA backbones without updating ForkCast. After adaptation on real-robot candidate rollouts, ForkCast also improves success over the base policy under both clean and visibility-limited conditions. Code will be released to benefit the research community.
authors: Chenru Wen, Huajian Zeng, Haokai Ding, Jian Kang, Anqing Duan, Dawei Zhou, Dezhen Song, Xingxing Zuo
bullets: Addresses manipulation failures caused by object slip and visual occlusion without retraining the VLA backbone.
Uses a candidate-conditioned world model to forecast common-horizon outcomes for Commit, Reobserve, and Replan.
A shared task-progress head selects whether to intervene and which recovery action to use, without a failure detector or intervention threshold.
On five simulated RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, pooled success increased from 13.3% to 30.0% for the frozen π₀.₅ policy.
Transferred to two additional VLA backbones and improved real-robot success under clean and visibility-limited conditions after candidate-rollout adaptation.

papers.title: ForkCast: Predictive Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Policies via Counterfactual Futures
papers.tldr: ForkCast enables a frozen vision-language-action policy to recover from slip and occlusion by comparing predicted outcomes of continuing, reobserving, or replanning.

papers.abstract: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs. In active inference, it can respond to an urgent need by increasing the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. We compare these two interventions, separately and together, in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, and ask how each changes survival, perception and the body model the agent learns. Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from their lethal boundaries and changes the states from which the agent learns, so its learned model covers fewer need levels, with lower quality across all levels but slightly higher quality on the levels it visits. An experiment on 72 further layouts does not establish the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts, but both interventions improve average survival there and their interaction is positive. Survival alone therefore gives an incomplete account of how a model prioritises needs and learns about its body.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies excel at generalist robotic manipulation but generate actions without explicitly modeling their environmental consequences. World action models (WAMs) incorporate future prediction, yet most rely on costly video generation, while latent alternatives either use predicted futures only as auxiliary targets or infer latent actions from suboptimal visual transitions through costly large-scale video pretraining. We introduce WAVE-0 (World-model-Augmented VLA Execution), a framework that bridges VLAs and WAMs through a lightweight latent world model. By connecting the semantic understanding of pretrained VLAs with explicit future prediction, WAVE-0 allows anticipated action consequences to directly guide action generation. Built on a pretrained VLA, its 257M world model translates VLM-generated latent action plans into predicted future representations that condition the action expert, unifying latent planning, future prediction, and action generation. The world model is trained directly on ground-truth robot actions with a counterfactual ranking objective, requiring neither pixel reconstruction nor large-scale video pretraining. WAVE-0 achieves success rates of 91.47% on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.7% on LIBERO, along with 88.0%, 61.4%, and 75.0% on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and LIBERO-Para, respectively. On real-world tasks, it improves the success rate of $\pi_{0.5}$ from 38.3% to 73.3%. These results demonstrate strong manipulation performance and generalization across diverse distribution shifts.
authors: Haomin Wang, Anqiong Ji, Ke Wang, Zhongshan Liu, Ru Ying, Ran Zheng, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit environmental consequence modeling in VLA policies without relying on costly video generation or large-scale video pretraining.
Uses a 257M-parameter world model to translate VLM-generated latent action plans into predicted future representations that condition action generation.
Trains the world model directly from ground-truth robot actions with a counterfactual ranking objective, avoiding pixel reconstruction.
Reports strong simulation performance across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and its distribution-shift variants.
Improves real-world success for π0.5 from 38.3% to 73.3%, demonstrating better generalization across distribution shifts.

papers.abstract: Latent world-model planning has shown promising results in goal-conditioned robotic manipulation, but remains challenging for long-horizon planning due to limited temporal guidance and inefficient action search. A distant visual goal provides little guidance for preparatory actions, while uninformed action sampling makes local optimization inefficient. We propose PILOT (Policy-Initialized Local Optimization with Temporal subgoals), which uses a video model to generate intermediate visual subgoals and a learned policy to initialize the cross-entropy method (CEM). CEM refines candidate action sequences toward each subgoal using an action-conditioned world model in a receding-horizon control loop. In our primary real-robot evaluation across four UR5e manipulation tasks, PILOT achieves 68.8% success, compared with 55.0% without policy initialization, 13.8% for policy-only execution, and 0.0% for direct final-goal planning. Simulation results show that these gains persist over longer horizons: PILOT exceeds direct execution of the same policy by 30 percentage points on long Push-T tasks and by 22 percentage points on LIBERO-10. Policy initialization also accelerates local optimization: on Push-T, CEM matches the cost reached by generic initialization after 10 iterations in only 4 iterations and reduces the final planning cost by 24.1% under the same sampling budget. These results show that combining temporal subgoals with policy-guided action search improves both long-horizon task execution and local planning efficiency. Videos are available on the webpage: https://pilot-planner.github.io/.
authors: Yang Liu, Hanchen Cui, Karthik Desingh

Simulation results indicate improved long-horizon execution and faster, lower-cost local optimization.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is severely under-constrained by limited X-ray projections. Learned reconstruction can provide complementary anatomical information, but using it as a prior in patient-specific Gaussian reconstruction introduces two challenges. First, the discrepancy between the learned prior and current reconstruction is spatially non-uniform: some local differences contain useful missing 3D information, whereas others reflect prior bias. Second, even a volumetrically beneficial correction can conflict with the observed X-ray measurements. Since X-ray measurements are line integrals, spatially separated corrections may affect overlapping rays, with their signed projection responses reinforcing or partially canceling in the measurement residual, so their feasibility cannot always be assessed independently. In this paper, we introduce RePrior, a multi-stage progressive prior-correction framework that addresses correction actionability, measurement feasibility, and representation expressivity. Selective Correction Proposal (SCP) first identifies actionable signed local corrections from prior--reconstruction discrepancies. Measurement-Constrained Reconciliation (MCR) then jointly enforces their consistency with patient-specific X-ray measurements, while Hybrid Residual Enhancement (HRE) recovers additional correction capacity through complementary voxel- and Gaussian-domain degrees of freedom around the reconciled anchor. RePrior requires neither test-time ground truth nor case-specific network fine-tuning. RePrior gains approximately 2.6~dB in 3D PSNR over R$^2$-Gaussian across LUNA16, PANORAMA, and PENGWIN. Beyond prior-assisted reconstruction, it delivers additional gains in volumetric quality and observed-view projection fidelity, with consistent gains in held-out-view fidelity in the backbone-matched evaluation.
authors: Mengrui Yin, Tianxingjian Ding, Wufan Zhao, Ziyang Yan, Yu Tian
bullets: Addresses spatially varying prior bias and conflicts between volumetric corrections and overlapping-ray measurements.

Requires neither test-time ground truth nor case-specific network fine-tuning.
Reports approximately 2.6 dB higher 3D PSNR than R²-Gaussian across LUNA16, PANORAMA, and PENGWIN.
Also improves volumetric quality, observed-view projection fidelity, and—under backbone-matched evaluation—held-out-view fidelity.

papers.abstract: Active exploration and semantic navigation require an embodied agent to build memory from partial observations, predict how the evolution of observed spatial memory may support future motion, and convert that prediction into actionable plans. We present GLAM, a goal-conditioned latent world model trained over global spatiotemporal memory, and GLAM NAV, the complete navigation system built around it. Given historical map tokens, a navigation goal, and the current robot pose, GLAM jointly predicts future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents, allowing future spatial context and navigation intent to be inferred in a shared representation space. The model follows a JEPA-like latent prediction paradigm, operates directly on map-level latent tokens rather than RGB reconstruction, and uses a pretrained waypoint encoder-decoder to supervise and decode navigation plans within GLAM NAV. Training data are collected by replaying ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat over HM3D v0.2 scene assets and slicing them into multi-timescale prediction samples. On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav subset reproduction setting, GLAM NAV improves over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline in both success rate and success weighted by path length.
bullets: Uses historical map tokens, the navigation goal, and robot pose to jointly predict future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents.
Applies JEPA-like latent prediction directly to map-level tokens instead of reconstructing RGB observations.
GLAM NAV combines the world model with a pretrained waypoint encoder-decoder to generate actionable navigation plans.
Trained on replayed ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat using HM3D v0.2 scenes and multi-timescale prediction samples.
On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav reproduction subset, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict actions and future observations, typically from a reconstruction-based representation that carries noisy, redundant information which can complicate downstream predictions. We introduce LeWAM, a bidirectional transformer for forward, backward, inverse dynamics and policy prediction, on a decoder-free JEPA latent trained end-to-end through all four modes. We see the following benefits: 1) Alignment: linear probes read robot and object state from LeWAM's latent better than from a regular Le World Model (a forward-only JEPA world model), while the latent ignores visual distractors as well as LeWM does and far better than a reconstruction-based WAM. 2) Acting: Closed-loop evaluations of LeWAM match a regular flow-matching policy trained on the same encoder at matched size, while also providing a world model. 3) Planning: Sampling raw actions when planning with WAMs lets MPC exploit dynamics-model inaccuracies; planning in the noise space of the policy head instead improves the closed-loop performance of these WAMs.

Closed-loop acting matches a same-size flow-matching policy while also providing a world model.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated locomotion and manipulation informed by future scene evolution and whole-body motion, yet learning these capabilities is constrained by scarce robot demonstrations. Human video and motion datasets offer scalable supervision, but many contain only video or motion rather than paired video-motion data. Moreover, human motion does not directly specify executable robot actions. We present Being-M0.7, a latent world-action model that transfers visual-motion priors learned from mixed-modality human data to humanoid control through pre-training, robot mid-training, and action post-training. We curate a corpus from more than 10,000 hours of raw human-centric data, integrating video-only, motion-only, and paired video-motion streams to learn complementary visual dynamics and whole-body kinematic structure. Joint prediction of future latent visual states and motion encourages visual representations to encode future kinematics. Robot mid-training adapts this coarse-grained prior to robot viewpoints and body dynamics. During action post-training, an action expert combines visual predictive representations from the frozen, adapted prior with current images and proprioception through gated cross-attention, grounding predictive context in executable whole-body commands. Being-M0.7 achieves the highest aggregate success rate among the compared baselines on SIMPLE and matches the strongest baseline on real-world Unitree G1 loco-manipulation tasks.
authors: Junpeng Yue, Boyuan Li, Yuxuan Wang, Zepeng Wang, Yuhui Fu, Feiyang Xie, Yu Zhang, Jing Zhang, Xianqi Zhang, Weibo Li, Xiaofei Zheng, Yuming Fang, Jiangxing Wang, Zongqing Lu

Pre-trains on mixed video-only, motion-only, and paired video-motion data, using joint future visual-state and motion prediction.
Adapts the learned prior to robot viewpoints and dynamics through robot mid-training.
An action expert combines frozen predictive representations with images and proprioception via gated cross-attention.
Achieves the highest aggregate success among compared baselines on SIMPLE and matches the strongest baseline on real-world Unitree G1 tasks.

papers.abstract: The diversity of robot embodiments and action spaces makes it challenging to build robot world models that generalize across different embodiments. We introduce the Latent Action-Conditioned Robot World Model (LAC-WM), which operates within a learned unified latent action space shared across diverse embodiments. This unified action space improves the world model's performance when adapted to previously unseen robot embodiments. We compare LAC-WM with an Explicit Action-Conditioned World Model (EAC-WM), which conditions on explicit motion labels. Our results show that explicit action conditioning leads to disjoint action representations across embodiments, limiting downstream performance when adapting to new robots. We evaluate both models on dexterous manipulation tasks and a modified LIBERO benchmark. LAC-WM improves downstream performance over EAC-WM by up to 46.7% on dexterous manipulation and 11.7% on LIBERO. Crucially, the unified latent action space allows LAC-WM's downstream performance to scale positively with the number of embodiments used during pretraining. In contrast, the disjoint action space in EAC-WM leads to decreased performance as the number of pretraining embodiments increases. These results highlight the importance of a unified action space for efficient cross-embodiment learning, addressing a key challenge in robotics. Project website: https://lacwm.github.io/
authors: Huang Huang, Sriram Yenamandra, Arjun Majumdar, Elie Aljalbout, Tushar Nagarajan, Tsung-Yen Yang, Akshara Rai, Michael Rabbat, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu, Tingfan Wu, Franziska Meier
bullets: Cross-embodiment diversity and differing action spaces hinder generalizable robot world models.
LAC-WM uses learned latent actions shared across embodiments, while EAC-WM uses explicit motion labels.
Evaluated on dexterous manipulation and a modified LIBERO benchmark.
LAC-WM improves downstream performance over EAC-WM by up to 46.7% and 11.7%, respectively.
Performance scales positively with more pretraining embodiments for LAC-WM, unlike EAC-WM.

figures.caption: Figure 1. LAC-WM Architecture. During pretraining (yellow area), the inverse dynamics model (IDM) encodes cross-embodiment image observations into a unified latent action space, as the condition for the forward dynamics model (FDM). A motion decoder translates the latent actions into motion labels, including delta human hand poses, robot end-effector actions, and camera motion. During finetuning (green area), an action projector encodes raw robot actions of unseen embodiments into the pre-trained unified latent action space.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine visual dynamics modeling with action generation, but their high inference latency limits responsive robot control. Recent efforts accelerate inference by removing explicit future-video generation at test time, as in FastWAM, an approach that requires a specially tailored architectural design. More general caching strategies exploit feature redundancy, but redundancy alone does not capture the changing computational demands of closed-loop control. To address these challenges, we present RealtimeWAM, a general, training-free framework that coordinates parallel execution with adaptive computation for low-latency inference across diverse WAM architectures. We exploit layerwise dependencies to overlap observation processing with prediction. However, concurrent branches still compete for GPU resources, limiting the benefit of parallel execution. We therefore adapt computation throughout the pipeline through selective reuse, caching observation features in visually stable regions and reusing Transformer residuals while reserving additional refinement for small predicted adjustments. We evaluate RealtimeWAM on FastWAM and OpenWAM across RoboTwin, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus. On an RTX 4090, measured mean inference latencies are 24.09 and 63.09 ms, corresponding to average speedups of 8.90$\times$ and 10.67$\times$. Average success rates are 82.75% and 87.41%, respectively, within 0.02 and 0.53 percentage points of native inference. Across five real-world tasks, RealtimeWAM improves average success rates over native inference by 17.2 and 37.2 percentage points on FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively.
bullets: Targets high WAM inference latency, which limits responsive closed-loop robot control.
Overlaps observation processing and prediction using layerwise dependencies, while managing GPU contention through adaptive computation.
Caches features in visually stable regions and reuses Transformer residuals, adding refinement only for small predicted changes.
Evaluated on FastWAM and OpenWAM across RoboTwin, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, achieving 24.09 ms and 63.09 ms mean latency with 8.90× and 10.67× speedups.
Maintains near-native benchmark success rates and improves average real-world task success by 17.2 and 37.2 percentage points for FastWAM and OpenWAM.
